description: A heap maintains the min or max element accessible in O(1), with O(log n) insert/remove — ideal whenever a problem repeatedly needs 'the smallest/largest remaining item' rather than a full sort, or needs to merge/rank streams of data.
important_details: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; pass a custom Comparator (or negate values) for a max-heap.
Using a heap to keep only the top K elements bounds space at O(k) instead of O(n) — pop the heap's top whenever size exceeds k.
Two heaps (a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half) give O(log n) median maintenance on a data stream.
K-way merge problems (multiple sorted lists/arrays) use a heap seeded with one element per source to get the next global minimum in O(log k).
other_relevant_details: Heap-based solutions are typically O(n log k) — much better than sorting the entire input (O(n log n)) when k is small relative to n. Recognize the pattern from 'kth largest/smallest', 'top k frequent', 'median of a stream', or 'merge k sorted'.

variations.description: Maintain a heap of exactly size k while scanning the input, evicting the least-relevant element whenever the heap grows past k, leaving exactly the top k at the end.
important_details: For 'k largest', use a MIN-heap of size k — the heap's root is always the smallest of the current top-k candidates, ready to be evicted.
For 'k smallest' or 'k closest', use a MAX-heap of size k for the symmetric reason.
This bounds heap operations to O(n log k), better than sorting all n elements when k << n.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log k). Space: O(k).

problems.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix

variations.description: Split the data stream into two balanced heaps — a max-heap holding the smaller half, a min-heap holding the larger half — so the median is always derivable from their tops in O(1).
important_details: Invariant: sizes of the two heaps differ by at most 1, and every element in the max-heap (lower half) is <= every element in the min-heap (upper half).
After every insertion, rebalance by moving an element between heaps if the size invariant or ordering invariant is violated.
If total count is odd, the median is the top of the larger heap; if even, it's the average of both tops.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log n) per insertion, O(1) per median query. Space: O(n).

variations.description: Merge k sorted lists/arrays into one sorted output by seeding a min-heap with one candidate element from each source, always extracting the global minimum and refilling from the source it came from.
important_details: Heap holds (value, sourceIndex, elementIndex) tuples so you know which source to pull the next candidate from after popping.
This generalizes pairwise merging (O(n*k)) down to O(n log k).
Also directly solves 'smallest range covering elements from k lists' with a small twist tracking the current max across heap contents.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log k) where N is total elements across all lists. Space: O(k) for the heap.

Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums

variations.description: Use a heap to always pick the globally best next task/interval/resource in a greedy simulation — common for CPU scheduling, meeting room allocation, and reorganizing strings to avoid adjacent repeats.
important_details: A max-heap of remaining task frequencies lets you always schedule the currently-most-frequent task next, which is the key greedy insight for cooldown-style scheduling.
A min-heap of interval end times tracks the earliest-freeing resource — used to count the minimum number of meeting rooms needed at any point.
Often paired with a cooldown queue or a secondary structure to enforce a 'wait period' before an item re-enters the heap.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log 26) which is effectively O(n) since heap size is bounded by alphabet size. Space: O(26).
